newsitem.title: USA: Homeowner heaven at Hardware Show.
newsitem.headline: Homeowner heaven at Hardware Show.

text.p: Ergonomic rakes and shovels, personalized bug zappers and an array of technology-driven products -- including an ultrasonic tape measure -- are here to make life easier, if not more expensive.
Whatever the hardware lover might want, it is here this week at the National Hardware Show.
Roughly one-quarter of a million products of all shapes, sizes and power are jammed together for viewing by 70,000 hardware professionals overseeing the $550 billion home improvement industry.
Even the simplest tools, the shovel and the hammer, have undergone makeovers.

Surrealist painter Salvador Dali appeared to have gotten into the designs of Ames Law and Garden Tools, which featured curved-handled rakes, shovels, hoes and cultivators for the formerly stoop-shouldered gardener.

The West Virginia garden tool maker consulted with an ergonomist, a physical therapist and a chiropracter to help formulate the long, curved handles that keep the user's back and legs in a more upright and relaxed position. For that, they doubled the price of the average rake to about $25.
Weeds and grass were under attack from an ever-more-powerful array of trimming devices, culminating in the "Grass Hog," a fearsome-looking weed whacker.
For those seeking the joys of nature in their backyard without the hassle, Companion Group advertised its "environmentally friendly" Personal Bug Zapper.

For $14.99 (including two double-A batteries), the device delivers a 1.5-volt shock to bugs caught by a wave of the small tennis raquet-like wand. The zapper could deliver a slight shock to a human, but makes for a quick, unfriendly death for mosquitoes.

"No pesticides and no sprays," Companion's Jolynn Elliott said of her company's electrified fly-swatter. "People think of the ultra-violet bug-zapper hanging away from the house, doing the job long-range. But if you're out reading in the yard and it gets a little buggy..."
If bugs or failing light finally drives one back inside, but you forget to turn on the porch light, Qwikset Corp. has the answer.
A tiny motion sensor in its new Night Sight ($85) lock activates when a person gets within three feet, turning on a glowing light around the lock and allowing for quick entry.
"No more leaving the porch light on so people know you're not at home," the company's Ron Fincher said.
Inside, a glance reveals a red light if the deadbolt is locked.

Qwikset, a unit of Black & Decker Corp, also displayed its remote house key, similar to those car-owners use to activate their car alarms. Eventually, Fincher said one remote key, which features a continuously rotating security code to prevent break-ins, would work on house, car and garage.
The motion sensor lock sells for $85, and the remote key lock for $290.

Once inside, a homeowner could feel safer in a microbe-free bathroom complete with Magnolia Co.'s Bacti-Check toilet seat. A substance inside the vinyl seat is advertised to kill germs presumably borne by visitors.

Magnolia, a privately held Columbus, Miss.-based company, said the germ-killing material in its $9 toilet seats was also gradually becoming available for glazes on toilet bowls and bathroom wall tiles.

For when the fixer-upper wants to measure a room for a new carpet or furniture, Bosch Power Tools showed off its ultrasonic measurer, which automatically computes square footage (or meters) with a push of a button.
Lining up floor tiles or ceiling molding without penciling in guidelines is easy with Bosch's laser levelers, which shoot a red beam around the room. The products are priced around $100 and up.
